address: 5646 Milton St. (North Central Expressway), Dallas, TX
recipient: Mr. & Mrs. Felix Yoder, Berne, Ind.
notes: Front caption: “Meadows Building, Dallas, Texas. Located on the North Central Expressway, the Meadows Building is unique in that it has the largest ‘hanging roof garden’ outside Rockefeller Center. The building covers six acres, has parking for 500 cars. Built by the employees of the General American Oil Co. of Texas as a trust for employee pensions. Color by John Messina.” Published by Texas Post Card Co., Dallas / made by Dexter, West Nyack, N.Y. Completed in 1955, the Meadows Building was the first Dallas office tower built outside downtown, designed by architect J.N. MacCammon and named for company president Algur H. Meadows; it was employee-owned through a 1950 pension trust, and its famous hanging garden (by Lambert Landscaping) was removed in 1984 and later restored in a 2020s renovation. 4-cent Lincoln stamp, postmarked Dallas, Tex., 7:30 PM, 30 Nov 1963 — just eight days after President Kennedy's assassination in Dallas on November 22, 1963. Message: “11-30-63. Dear Folks: We got here about 9:00 Thursday morn. OK but tired. It started to rain just before we got to Texas and rained gently the rest of the way. We are seeing the place that saddened the nation. The girls are trying hard to make our stay pleasant. Sam's went on south this morning. Expecting to start for home next Wed morning. Love Dad & Mother” — “the place that saddened the nation” almost certainly refers to Dealey Plaza and the assassination site, making this an ordinary family road-trip card caught up in the immediate aftermath of a defining national tragedy.
feed_description: A Dallas postcard mailed just eight days after JFK's assassination — ‘we are seeing the place that saddened the nation,’ a family writes home from the Meadows Building.

location: Nashville, Tennessee — Parthenon and Lake, Centennial Park
address: Parthenon, Centennial Park, West End Ave & 25th Ave N, Nashville, TN
recipient: Mr. Wilbur Wallace, Woodland Christian Church, Lexington, Ky.
notes: Front is a black-and-white night photograph captioned “Parthenon and Lake, Centennial Park, Nashville, Tennessee,” showing the illuminated Parthenon replica reflected in Lake Watauga. Back printed text: “Lake Watauga lies at the foot of the beautiful terrace in Centennial Park which is crowned by the classic Parthenon said to be the perfect replica of the famous Parthenon of ancient Greece. The lake was named in honor of the first settlers of Tennessee, who were known as the Watauga, or Cumberland settlers. They came to Tennessee in 1769.” Photo copyright by Wiles—Photographers; “A ‘Natural Finish’ Card Made by Graycraft Card Co., Danville, Va.” Both the Parthenon and Lake Watauga date to Nashville’s 1897 Tennessee Centennial Exposition; when the fair closed, the city kept both as permanent fixtures after acquiring the grounds in 1902–03, stocking the lake with fish soon after. 1-cent green Franklin stamp, postmarked Nashville, Tenn., Jun 17, 1948. Message: “I am in the city for the day. Brought Mal[e?] to 7:00 A.M. bus. I am going to Cottontown this P.M. to stay until I hear where you want to visit first, Nov. 5-6. I do not have any more. Love, Mother.” (the name after “Brought” resists a confident reading). Cottontown is a real small community in Sumner County just north of Nashville — a nice bit of local color. Addressed to a Woodland Christian Church in Lexington, Kentucky, with a note “(Mr. Parish)” beside the address whose exact function isn't fully clear — possibly indicating the church's minister.
feed_description: A 1948 postcard of Nashville's illuminated Parthenon reflected in Lake Watauga, with a mother writing to her son's church in Lexington, Kentucky about a stop in Cottontown, TN.

recipient: Court House Gang, Warsaw, Missouri, c/o Art Call
notes: Front: “Greetings from Hoover Dam” — a color photo looking down the canyon at the dam's downstream face, with two women in the foreground and an American flag flying over the intake towers. Back printed text: “HOOVER DAM. Looking towards the outlet tunnels and huge powerhouse below the world's highest dam. This $125,000,000 project is one of man's greatest engineering achievements. Height 727 feet above bedrock, crest 1,244 feet, and 660 feet thick at the base. Photo by Don Lidikay Union Pacific R.R.” Published by Western Resort Publications, Santa Ana, Calif.; copyright Ferris H. Scott. Card codes FS-470 / S-16839-11. 5-cent Washington stamp, postmarked Las Vegas, Nev., Feb 14, 1966. Message: “Feb. 14. Arrived in Las Vegas Sat. 6:00 PM. Nice trip. Rudy” — a quick, cheerful travel update, addressed collectively to the “Court House Gang” back home at the Warsaw, Missouri courthouse (county seat of Benton County) — a charming glimpse of small-town office camaraderie.
feed_description: A 1966 Valentine's Day postcard from Las Vegas — Rudy sends quick greetings from Hoover Dam to the whole ‘Court House Gang’ back in Warsaw, Missouri.

location: Allenstein, East Prussia (now Olsztyn, Poland) — Castle
notes: Front caption: “Allenstein. Partie am Schloß” — a hand-tinted photo of Allenstein Castle's distinctive red tower and Gothic brick hall beside a tree-lined canal. The castle is a 14th-century Teutonic Order stronghold (Ordensburg), begun around 1347–53 as the administrative seat of the Warmia cathedral chapter. Its most famous resident was the astronomer Nicolaus Copernicus, who lived here as chapter administrator from 1516–1521 and personally organized the town's successful defense during a Teutonic Knights' siege in 1520–21. Allenstein was German territory (East Prussia) when this card was sent; after WWII it was transferred to Poland and renamed Olsztyn, its German population expelled in 1945. This is a Feldpost (military field-post) card, exempt from postage under wartime rules, postmarked Allenstein, 13 October 1917 — deep in WWI, about a year before the Armistice. The address and message are both written sideways, running up the card rather than across. Address (partially legible): “Feldpost. Frau Martha [surname illegible], Berlin,” with what may be an old Berlin postal-district code alongside it. The message, in dense wartime cursive, opens “Liebe Frau!” (“Dear wife!” or “Dear Mrs. [name]!”) and seems to touch on travel and field-post/airmail arrangements, but honestly resisted a confident line-by-line transcription even after repeated review — the handwriting leans on a heavily abbreviated, period Kurrentschrift-influenced style. It's signed by several names at the bottom, including what looks like a cavalry rank abbreviation (“Ulan.”, short for Ulanen — lancer cavalry) followed by names including “P. Kaatz” and “Paul Nasser,” with at least one more only partly legible — suggesting a joint greeting from a group of soldier comrades to one of their wives back home. Flagging the body of this one honestly as only partially deciphered; a reader fluent in old German military cursive would likely get more out of it.
feed_description: A WWI Feldpost card from Allenstein Castle (now Olsztyn, Poland) — once Copernicus's home base — signed by a group of soldiers sending greetings to a wife back in Berlin, October 1917.

location: Salt Lake City, Utah — Brigham Young's Grave
address: Brigham Young Family Cemetery, 140 East 1st Avenue, Salt Lake City, UT
recipient: Mrs. Viola Berry[?] (surname could also read “Berney”), Breckenridge P.O., Caldwell Co., Missouri
notes: Front: “1003. Brigham Young's Grave, Salt Lake City, Utah” — a tinted photo of the ornate wrought-iron-fenced tomb of Brigham Young (1801–1877), second president of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, who led the Mormon pioneers into the Salt Lake Valley in 1847 and served as the first governor of Utah Territory. He's buried in a small private family cemetery just northeast of Temple Square, alongside other family members and early Church figures. Back: published by The Thayer Publishing Co., Denver, Colo., with the printed reassurance “THIS SPACE CAN BE USED FOR A WRITTEN MESSAGE, USING ONE-CENT STAMP” — the kind of note publishers commonly added right after the U.S. Post Office's March 1907 rule change permitting a divided back (message and address sharing one side). Paired with the 1-cent green Franklin stamp of that same general era, this points to a card from roughly 1907 into the early 1910s, though the postmark itself is too worn to confirm an exact year. Message: “Well how are you. I am at Depot at Salt Lake. am well had to-Lay over Train. Late Every thing shut down in my Business. if I can't get to business in Colorado will be home soon. Your as Ever R H Berry” — the writer delayed en route on a train layover, business plans up in the air. Addressed to “Mrs. Viola Berry” (the surname could also be read as “Berney” — genuinely hard to resolve, though “Berry” would match the sender's own signature), “Breckenridge P.O., Caldwell Co., Mo.” — Breckenridge is a real small town in Caldwell County already familiar from a couple of other cards in the archive.
feed_description: An undated early-1900s postcard of Brigham Young's grave in Salt Lake City — a traveler stuck on a train layover writes home to Breckenridge, Missouri.

recipient: Robert Bowman, 123 West Main, Shelbyville, Il. 62565
notes: Front: a twilight photo of Fort Worth's downtown skyline reflected in a pond, titled simply “FORT WORTH” in bold magenta script — the kind of minimalist, photo-forward postcard design common in the 1980s. Back: “Fort Worth, Texas,” published by The Texas Postcard Company, Plano, TX (card F-116); printed by McGrew Color Graphics, Kansas City, Mo. (a postcard printer active from at least the 1970s onward); photo by Richard Stockton. No postmark or stamp is present — this card appears to have never gone through the mail, likely tucked into an envelope or handed over directly. Pencilled dealer/collector marks “1595” and “100” appear at the top — the same “1595” marking that has now turned up on more than one card in this collection, suggesting several of these postcards passed through the same dealer lot at some point. Message: “Hi! We are having a good time. Saw [?] graduate & also his[?] signed diploma. See you sometime. Student, Fred, Linda & Christy” — a few words here resist full confidence, but the gist is a graduation trip update. Addressed to Robert Bowman in Shelbyville, Illinois — the ZIP code (62565) confirms the card postdates 1963, and the skyline view is consistent with 1980s-era Fort Worth.
feed_description: An undated Fort Worth skyline postcard, never mailed — Fred, Linda & Christy write to Robert Bowman in Shelbyville, Illinois about a graduation trip.

location: Hector Falls, New York (near Watkins Glen)
address: Hector Falls, east shore of Seneca Lake, north of Watkins Glen, NY
recipient: Mrs. Lena Stafford, 71 Montreal St., Sanford, Maine 04073
notes: Front: a color photo of Hector Falls, a multi-tiered cascade over layered shale, framed by trees with a wooden viewing rail at the base. Back printed text: “Hector Falls — Is a sparkling gem, as it cascades over the rocky slope above the east shore of Seneca Lake, a few miles north of Watkins Glen, N.Y.” Published by Howard Champion, Watkins Glen, N.Y.; “Lustrachrome” process card made by Tichnor Bros., Inc., Boston. 6-cent Flag over White House stamp (first issued January 1968), postmark mostly illegible beyond a partial “...R. N.Y.” Combined with the ZIP code on the address (04073, Sanford, Maine, confirming a post-1963 date) and the 6¢ Flag stamp's common-use window, this card likely dates to around 1968–1971. Message: “Dear Staffy – Polly and I are on a trip to see the Burpees in New York. We went to this spot yesterday and hope to go to Niagara Falls before we come home. However the weather is not too good. Hope to be home by Wednesday. Time will tell. Much love, ‘Ma’ Hadden[s]” — a warm travel update from one older woman to another, touring the Finger Lakes region with a stop planned for Niagara Falls before heading home.
feed_description: A postcard from Hector Falls near Watkins Glen, NY — ‘Ma’ Hadden writes to a friend in Sanford, Maine about a Finger Lakes trip with a Niagara Falls stop still to come.

recipient: Herrn Albert Hueske, 509 Ave of Oaks, Houston, Tex. 77009, U.S.A.
notes: This card came in filed as “Unknown” — the front carries no printed caption — but the return address on the back gives it away: this is Trappenkamp itself. The aerial front photo shows a purpose-built settlement of identical red-roofed apartment blocks laid out along straight streets, ringed by heathland and forest with dunes and open water visible in the distance. Trappenkamp has a striking origin story: the town didn't exist before the 1930s. The site began as “Gönnebeker Heide,” a Prussian cavalry and infantry parade ground; in July 1934 the German Navy chose the site (by then state forest) to build a mine-storage depot relieving pressure on the naval arsenal at Kiel. British troops occupied it on 18 May 1945, and afterward it was repurposed as a refugee camp for Germans expelled from the eastern territories and the Sudetenland. It became its own independent municipality in April 1956, having previously been administered as part of neighboring Bornhöved. The front photo captures exactly this transformation — a former military depot reborn as row after row of refugee housing. The return address, written by the sender at the top of the card per German convention, reads “2351 Trappenkamp / Arndtstr. 31” — “2351” is an old West German four-digit postal code, consistent with a mid-20th-century date. A printed clearance code at the bottom, “Frei. Reg. Präs. Düss. 17-C 208,” is the kind of official image-rights approval stamp West German postcard publishers commonly carried at the time. Message (German): “Unser lieber Vetter Albert! Gottes Segen für Dein neues Lebensjahr, viel Glück, Freude u. Gesundheit für Dich u. Hildegard. Wo das X auf der Karte, in der Richtung wohnen wir. Viel schöne Stunden wünschen Euch in Liebe Eure Werner u. Hemchen.” Translation: “Our dear cousin Albert! God's blessing for your new year of life [i.e. happy birthday], much luck, joy and health for you and Hildegard. Where the X is on the card, that's the direction we live in. Wishing you many lovely hours, with love, your Werner and Hemchen.” Addressed to Albert Hueske at 509 Ave of Oaks, Houston, Texas — the very same street address as the Brauer family's Laredo postcard already in the archive (card #184) — very likely the same household or a close relative, both maintaining ties with German family back home. Worth a look for the Family Networks tag.
feed_description: A birthday greeting from Trappenkamp, Germany — a town built from a WWII naval depot turned refugee settlement — to cousin Albert Hueske at the same Houston address as another card already in the archive.
